analysis.one_liner: Bars federal regulators from ever requiring companies to report their supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Scope 3 Act would have written into law that no securities regulator can require a public company to disclose the greenhouse gas emissions of its supply chain — the emissions produced by its suppliers, shipping, and customers, known as 'Scope 3'. Companies would be permanently shielded from having to account for those emissions to investors or the public. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, received no hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies — especially oil and gas producers and other energy-intensive businesses — gain the most. They avoid the cost of measuring and reporting supply-chain emissions, and avoid the reputational and investor pressure that such disclosures can create. Emissions in the supply chain often dwarf what a company reports from its own operations, so keeping them off the books leaves investors and the public with a much smaller picture of a company's climate footprint.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public companies, especially oil and gas

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any requirement, under the securities laws, that a company disclose the greenhouse gas emissions of its value chain (Scope 3 emissions) [S2] [S3].
The ban would apply to the securities regulators generally, not just to a pending SEC rule, so it would block future administrations from reinstating such a disclosure requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors and the public. Shareholders increasingly use emissions data to price climate risk, and Scope 3 emissions are often the largest share of a company's footprint. Without disclosure, they cannot see that risk. The public also loses a basic transparency tool for judging whether companies' climate claims match their supply chains.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue in good faith that Scope 3 reporting is expensive and unreliable, since it requires estimating emissions produced by suppliers and customers a company does not control, and falls hardest on smaller suppliers who must produce data for many large customers [S3].

Critics of the bill note that supply-chain emissions are frequently the majority of a company's total climate impact, and that banning disclosure across the board removes the ability of investors — who own these companies — to see the risks they are underwriting [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real compliance concern — the difficulty and cost of estimating emissions a company does not directly control — for a blanket prohibition. A narrower fix, such as phasing in disclosure for the largest emitters first, was not what the bill offered. The cost falls on transparency itself: investors and the public would permanently lose visibility into the largest share of corporate climate impact, to the benefit of the companies being asked to report it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Nehls introduced the bill on July 26, 2022, with 14 original cosponsors — 12 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies the bill would have protected — particularly large emitters who would have faced the cost and exposure of supply-chain emissions reporting — are better off, since the ban never passed but the disclosure requirement was also never enacted into statute during this Congress. The Securities and Exchange Commission's climate-disclosure work proceeded without this statutory prohibition, but the bill's death left the underlying fight over disclosure rules to be resolved elsewhere.

for.name: Rep. Troy Nehls
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit any securities-law requirement that companies disclose supply-chain emissions.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors (12 Republicans, 2 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; none of the bill's support went beyond that.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.role: Committee of referral; chair never scheduled a markup or hearing
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or markup.

against.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
against.what_they_did: Was developing a climate-disclosure rule for public companies that the bill was written to foreclose; the agency is the target of the bill's prohibition.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 14 cosponsors, 12 were Republicans and 2 were Democrats (Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar of Texas); the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and other energy-intensive public companies
industries.note: The bill would spare them from ever having to report supply-chain emissions, which are typically the largest share of their climate footprint. The savings come out of investors' and the public's ability to see that footprint.

industries.industry: ESG data providers and climate-analytics firms
industries.note: A blanket prohibition on required Scope 3 disclosure would remove the regulatory demand that underpins part of their market for emissions data and ratings.
